lesson_title: One Machine: the Bookkeeping Cycle, Rebuilt for the Exam
hook_text: Ten topics? No. Your whole Accounting year is ONE machine — and it fits in a shoebox.
clip_script: Picture the shoebox every small shop keeps: every scrap of paper from the month tossed inside — till tapes, invoices, credit notes, EFT stubs. Bookkeeping begins as a SORTING job. Six boxes on the table, and every slip belongs in exactly one. Money came in — receipts box. Money went out — payments box. Sold on trust — invoice-out. Customer brought goods back — credit-note box. Bought on trust — invoice-in. Sent goods back — debit-note box. Two questions sort every slip: did cash move, or a promise? And which way did the value travel? Sort the month and the chaos becomes six tidy piles — and each pile is a journal, already totalled, ready for the ledger. Then the weigh-in: every entry was an equal pair, so the debits and credits must weigh the same — twenty-six thousand each side, level scale, honest month. That is the whole year: sort the slips, write the diaries, gather the ledger, weigh the scale, count the street twice. One machine. Every exam question is just new slips.
visual_style: Overhead shoebox spilling paper slips that fly into six glowing boxes, piles morphing into journal columns, then a balance scale settling perfectly level on 26 000 and 26 000.
mood: Order-from-chaos satisfying — revision as seeing the whole machine at once.
pacing: Rapid sorting montage, a beat of stillness on the level scale, confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and rebuild the machine before your final exams.
